title: The garden owners
hookLine: owners of a garden plan to harvest before the poor come, and find it burned (68:17–33)

cards: It's the night before harvest. A garden full of fruit, heavy on the branches. The owners, brothers in the commentators' retelling, sit together and make a plan.
Tomorrow, early, before anyone's awake, we go out and pick it all. Quietly. And they swear to it.
No poor person gets through the gate today. They go to bed pleased with themselves. They don't know that something is already moving through their garden in the dark.

teach.b: Surah al-Qalam, verses seventeen to thirty-three. The owners swore they'd harvest in the morning, and the Qur'an adds a small detail: they made no exception.
Commentators understand that as: they didn't say in sha' Allah, if God wills. They spoke as if tomorrow was theirs.
While they slept, a visitation from their Lord passed over the garden, and by morning it was like a field already reaped, black, stripped.

At dawn they called to one another and set out, whispering on the road: let no needy person come in on you today. They arrived, and at first they didn't recognize it. We must have lost our way, they said.
Then: no, we've been deprived. Then the turn. The middlemost of them, the most balanced one, says: didn't I tell you?
Why didn't you glorify Allah? And they did: glory to our Lord, we were wrong. Then they turned on each other, blaming.

teach.h: WE WERE THE ONES WHO OVERSTEPPED.
teach.b: Then they admitted it together: we were the ones who overstepped.
And they ended with hope: perhaps our Lord will give us something better in its place. The Qur'an doesn't say where this garden was or who the men were.

Commentators tell a fuller story: the garden belonged to a good man in Yemen who always left a share for the poor, and after he died his sons decided to stop. That backstory comes from the commentaries, not the verses.
But the verses are clear enough. They lost the whole harvest trying to keep the poor's share. And the story doesn't end in the ashes.
It ends in repentance and hope.

how: Muslims give zakat on harvests and wealth and voluntary charity (sadaqah); saying in sha' Allah, if God wills, of future plans follows 18:23–24, and the story of the garden owners is told to teach both.

a promise to share the harvest with everyone
not saying 'if God wills' about tomorrow's plans

games.q: you're one of the owners, standing in front of a blackened garden. your brother says: didn't I tell you? what do you do?
o: glorify Allah and admit the wrong.
go home and plan the next harvest.
games.why: they said glory to our Lord, we were wrong, then blamed each other, then admitted it together and hoped for better.

practice: Think of something you'll receive or use today: a paycheck, a meal, a bag of groceries, a free hour.
Picture setting aside a small part before you start, not from the leftovers but from the top: a coin, a plate for a neighbor, ten minutes for someone who needs it. Decide what that share is.

wordCard.voice: No exception. In 68:17–33 the garden owners swore to harvest by morning without saying if God wills, lost everything overnight, and returned in repentance. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic, 68:18: and they made no exception, understood as not saying in sha' Allah.

carryVoice: Your line: the poor's share first. From the top, not the leftovers. Day six hundred forty-two, done.
